result: {"findings": [{"file": "src/runtime.zig", "line": 778, "severity": "major", "category": "correctness", "title": "Tick retune reads a snapshot that `poll` does not always refresh", "body": "The new comment claims \"every path above ends in a `loop.poll`, which refreshes it on return\". `Loop.poll` (src/ev/loop.zig:1387-1392) returns at `if (self.done()) return;` BEFORE either `updateNow` call. `done()` is true whenever `state.stopped` is set or the loop has no active completions and no queued completions — exactly the pure CPU-bound case the loop code itself calls out at src/ev/loop.zig:1420. On an executor whose loop is in that state (a worker in `until_stopped` mode running task batches with no I/O in flight), `loop.now()` is never refreshed and stays frozen at whatever `Loop.init` (src/ev/loop.zig:548) stored. Two consequences follow: (1) at line 784 `elapsed` is `tick_now -| tick_started_at` where line 791 assigned `tick_started_at = tick_now` from the same frozen snapshot, so `elapsed` is 0 on every pass; `task_ns_ewma` decays toward 0 and `tick_task_budget` pins at `max_tick_budget` (8192), so the adaptive tick tuning is dead. (2) `spendQuantum` (line 679) still reads the real clock and subtracts the frozen `tick_started_at`, so its `elapsed` is enormous and `tick_expired` is set at the first checkpoint of every batch, capping every batch at `checkpoint_interval` (127) quanta instead of at the measured ~100us target. The previous `Timestamp.now(.monotonic)` had neither problem. Note also that `Loop.now()` is documented as \"Get the current monotonic timestamp\" (src/ev/loop.zig:600) while it returns `state.now[0]`, the cached scan snapshot; that doc is what makes this substitution look safe."}, {"file": "src/ev/loop.zig", "line": 385, "severity": "major", "category": "correctness", "title": "New `updateNow` comment claims owner-thread-only, but `setTimer` calls it cross-thread", "body": "The added comment says `updateNow` is \"Owner-thread only, so no timer lock: the cross-thread `clearTimer` never reads `now`/`tick`.\" `clearTimer` is not the only cross-thread timer entry point. `Loop.setTimer` (line 622) calls `self.state.updateNow()` at line 636 and then `armTimer` -> `nowFor` (lines 420, 398), both of which write `tick`, `now[]` and `now_tick[]`. `setTimer` is exercised from a non-owner thread by the tree's own regression test, src/ev/test/timer.zig:288, whose comment at line 241 states \"this thread only uses the thread-safe setTimer/clearTimer/wake APIs, exactly like a migrated task's timedWaitClock does.\" The comment also contradicts the `timer_mutex` doc at line 269: \"Protects all timer heaps and the cached `now` values.\"\n\nMechanism: `poll` now performs two unlocked `updateNow` calls (lines 1392 and 1429) while another thread may be inside `setTimer` holding `timer_mutex` and mutating the same non-atomic `tick`/`now`/`now_tick` fields. This is a data race that TSan will report. It is also observable: with the interleaving B(setTimer) `tick +%= 1`, A(poll) `tick +%= 1` and `now[0] = t_a`, B `now[0] = t_b; now_tick[0] = tick`, the awake snapshot can end up holding the older of the two readings while tagged with the current tick, so `armTimer` for a `.duration` awake timer computes a backdated deadline from it — the same class of defect the regression test at src/ev/test/timer.zig:303 exists to prevent. The pre-existing post-poll `updateNow` was already unlocked, so the diff widens the window rather than opening it, but the comment asserts the very invariant that would justify the unlocked call and that invariant is false.
